summary.text: 没 is the standardized simplified form of 沒. The traditional graph is recorded with the meaning “sink” or “drown”; its common reading méi means “not have.” A sound-based borrowing of the graph for this different word has been proposed, but the older word’s sound and the proposed match remain unverified.

formation.text: The construction of traditional 沒 remains unsettled. The received 說文 analyzes it as 水 plus 𠬸, and later commentary assigns 𠬸 a sound role; another account describes a hand reaching into water. The available evidence does not resolve these competing explanations or establish 𠬸’s historical sound relation to 沒.

history.text: 没 is identified as the standardized simplified form of 沒 and is also classified as a variant. A variant-dictionary account says the right side of an older form was commonly corrupted into 殳 in a俗 form; this does not establish a complete graphic sequence for standardized 没. The related form 𣳚 is described as stroke-reduced, but its cited inscription is undated and does not establish a sequence leading to 没.

uncertainties.text: The hand-in-water picture and the analysis of 沒 as 水 plus 𠬸 are competing explanations; the original construction remains unsettled.
Later commentary assigns 𠬸 a sound role, but its reading and historical sound relation to 沒 remain unverified.

The origin and chronology of méi “not have” remain unresolved. The graph for “sink/drown” may have been reused for this different word because the words may have sounded alike, but the older word’s sound and proposed match are unverified. Other proposals involving 勿, 未, or 有 are contested.

senses.text: The received 說文 glosses 沒 as 沈, “sink” or “submerge”; dictionary accounts also record sinking and drowning. The use is documented, but its earliest attestation and the graph’s original meaning are not established.
Historical commentary cites uses of 沒 meaning “end” or “exhausted”; the earliest attestation of this sense is unresolved.

In the common reading méi, 沒 is used for “not have” and “none.” The graph may have been reused to write this different word because the words may have sounded alike; the older word’s sound, proposed match, borrowing path, and first use remain unresolved.

limitations.text: The cited examples for “sink” and “end/exhausted” were not independently dated, so the earliest attestations of these senses remain unresolved.
No primary textual evidence establishes the first use of méi “not have” or the proposed sound-based borrowing path.
